title: Browser AI Gets Faster: 200+ GPU Kernels, Not Precompiled but Generated On-Device
dek: There is no universal optimal kernel for AI in the browser: a kernel is an operator's implementation on specific hardware, and the optimum differs by device. The 200+ kernels are not hardcoded programs but templates generated in the browser for your device.
why: An 11-minute solo launch demo, no back-and-forth, medium density. The point that kernels must be tailored per device comes across intuitively; what is worth a close look is the templated-kernel mechanism and the Fleet crowdsourced tuning.
who: Engineers running LLMs in the browser and building high-performance frontend AI applications, plus technical decision-makers watching WebGPU and WASM local-inference approaches.
skip: The code walkthrough in the opening demo and the release-channel intro at the end can be sped up; focus on the kernel template mechanism and the Fleet data feedback loop.

points.h: Operators define, kernels run on hardware
points.body: The transcript first separates two concepts: a model is a big graph of operators, and an operator is just a mathematical definition — addition is A+B; a kernel is the implementation that lands that definition on specific hardware. The same add goes through WebGPU / WGSL in the browser, and corresponds to a CUDA or Metal kernel in other ecosystems. The two are often conflated, but the speed difference comes precisely from the latter: only if the underlying kernel is fast can the whole inference graph be fast. This also explains why it is worth repeatedly polishing a kernel for a simple operation instead of vaguely tuning a "general math library".

points.h: What ships is Jinja templates, not hardcoded kernels
points.body: The difference in approach is worth noting: the repository does not hold hardcoded WGSL files one by one, but a number of Jinja templates with if/else branches describing different devices. At execution time, the library validates the template, picks the appropriate data type and workgroup size, then renders it into the WGSL best suited to the current GPU adapter and runs it. For example, the same addition function: on the left the data type is narrow and the workgroup small; on the right, because the device supports a wider data type and a larger workgroup, the same add runs faster. The official release lists 200-plus kernel entries, but what is actually delivered is the ability to make kernels on the fly for the hardware.

points.h: Attention in the browser takes only about 20 lines of JS
points.body: The demo brings the abstraction back to practice: running a small piece of attention in the browser took only about 20 lines of JavaScript. The flow is text→token→vector, but a token's vector cannot be viewed independently; you have to look at how other tokens in the context affect it. All the code does is pull in four kernels from the Hub — matmul, softmax, add, layer normalization — and the rest of the scheduling and GPU data exchange is hidden by the Hugging Face Kernels library. The heavy lifting is all at the kernel layer, which is why the barrier to "doing local inference in the browser" has dropped.

points.h: The whole wave animation is really just one matrix multiplication
points.body: The same demo gives an intuitive comparison: 128 waves crossing a 1024×1024 matrix, where the color of every cell is an RGBA computed by a matrix multiplication. The animation of more than a million pixels on screen runs at about 60fps under WebGPU — 60 is not the compute ceiling, it is just requestAnimationFrame locking rendering to 60; the kernel itself can compute at about 400fps. Run the same logic in plain JavaScript and the frame rate drops to roughly 6.75fps. The gap is not in the math but in whether someone wrote it as an implementation hugging this GPU — which is exactly what that batch of kernels does.

points.h: Fleet turns user devices into a tuning data source via benchmarks
points.body: On the surface Fleet is a benchmark page: anyone can run their own GPU and see how it compares. But the project team says it plainly: the team only has the few devices on hand, while the real world has thousands upon thousands of WebGPU devices, and there may be edge cases they never thought of — some kernel performs poorly on your machine, or even fails outright. Fleet collects run data from real devices back for further optimization, and the optimized kernels return to all users because the project is open source. When you click Run Benchmark once, you are not just looking at a score, you are running a round of real-world adaptation testing for the project.
